module8: Tenant health audit and admin handover
Once the tenant is running, an audit shows what has drifted. A good handover lets a new admin take over without surprises.
Audit users and roles: find unused accounts, shared passwords and too many top-level admins.
Audit sharing, mail rules and device policies against your written baseline.
Score each area as pass, fix soon or fix now, and give every finding an owner and a date.
Prepare a handover pack: access list, policy list, recovery steps and a calendar of regular tasks.

An audit finds 14 accounts with no sign-in for 120 days, 6 global admins and one site shared with anyone who has the link. The team disables the old accounts, cuts admins to 2 and changes the link to named guests with expiry.
Audit a practice tenant using a checklist of 15 items. Produce a table of findings with a rating, an owner and a fix date, plus a one-page handover note.
All 15 items checked; every finding rated and owned; handover note lets a new admin find roles, policies and recovery steps.
quiz: Why should a tenant have only two or three global admins?
A top-level account can change everything, so each extra one is a bigger target and a bigger risk of mistakes. Everyone else gets a smaller role that fits their task.
A user leaves on Friday at 5 pm. List the main steps in order.
Block sign-in, reset sessions, convert or keep the mailbox for the agreed time, move files to the manager and remove the licence. Do them from the leaver checklist.
What is the benefit of a shared mailbox over sharing one password?
Each agent signs in with their own account, so access is tracked and can be removed one person at a time. A shared password gives no record of who did what.
Explain in one line each what SPF, DKIM and DMARC do.
SPF lists the servers allowed to send for your domain. DKIM signs each message so it can be proven genuine. DMARC tells receivers what to do when a check fails.
A site is shared with anyone who has the link. Is that a problem and what would you change?
Yes, because the link can be forwarded to anyone. Change to named guests only and set the access to expire, for example after 30 days.
A sign-in comes from a new country at 3 am. Which control should react?
A conditional access policy should ask for a second proof or block the sign-in. Multi-factor sign-in stops most stolen-password attacks.
A script will create 200 users from a file. What checks make this safe?
Have someone review the file and the script, test on a few rows first and keep a list of the created accounts so they can be removed if something is wrong.
A file labelled Confidential is attached to an email going outside the company. What should a data-loss rule do?
Block the message or warn the sender and log the event, depending on the rule. The test file in the exercise should be blocked.
You must find out who deleted a shared folder last week. Where do you look?
Search the audit log by date, activity type and site. The result shows the user, the time and the action.
Compare a tenant audit with a monthly health report, and say what an audit adds.
The monthly report tracks a few numbers over time. An audit checks every area against the written baseline and gives each finding a rating, an owner and a fix date.
ladder: L1 Basic: find your way
Remember the main menus of the admin centre and what each one is for. Identify where users, groups, billing and service health are shown. Recognise why only a few people hold the top role.
Give a ten minute tour and ask learners to find a user and a licence. Check they can say what a group is. A common mistake is clicking into settings without knowing what they change.
L2 Awareness: understand the risks
Understand why a stolen password is the most common way in. Explain what multi-factor sign-in and sharing limits protect. Describe the joiner, mover and leaver idea.
Use a short story of a leaver who still had access. Ask what could go wrong. Watch for learners who think a strong password alone is enough.
L3 Foundation: do the standard tasks
Apply the checklist to create a user, assign a licence, add a group and set up a shared mailbox. Reset a password safely. Follow the steps in order every time.
Let learners complete each task on a practice tenant. Check licences and group membership afterwards. Common mistake: giving extra roles to make a problem go away.
L4 Practitioner: run daily operations
Apply mail rules, sharing limits and device checks across a small company. Analyse a sign-in report and spot odd behaviour. Fix access problems without raising the role.
Give a case with three user complaints. Ask learners to find the cause for each. Common mistake: changing many settings at once, so the real fix is unknown.
L5 Specialist: design the security baseline
Analyse risks and design sign-in, device and data protection policies. Create labels and rules and test them on a pilot group. Keep a safe emergency account.
Ask learners to explain each policy in one sentence for a non-technical manager. Check the pilot results. Common mistake: forgetting the emergency account and locking everyone out.
L6 Advanced: audit and improve
Evaluate the whole tenant against a written baseline. Compare findings by risk and effort, and give each an owner and date. Review audit logs to answer who did what and when.
Give a messy practice tenant and a checklist. Check that ratings match the evidence. Common mistake: listing problems without owners or deadlines.
L7 Super expert: govern the tenant

Create a governance pack with admin roles by task, reviewed scripts for bulk changes, a monthly report and a recovery plan. Evaluate trade-offs between safety and ease of use. Teach others to run the tenant safely.
Ask for a pack another admin could use on day one. Check the rollback list and recovery test. Common mistake: scripts run without a review or a way back.
